snippets.text: Giant cell tumor of bone (GCTB) is a primary bone tumor that predominantly occurs in young adults aged 20–40 years, with a relatively high incidence in females. It is most commonly found in peripheral bones such as the knee and radius. The sacrum is the most common site for GCTB in the axial skeleton. In the spine, GCTB accounts for 2–3% of all spinal tumors, with a predilection for the cervical and sacral vertebrae. Although it is defined as benign, 5–10% of GCTBs exhibit local aggressiveness and a tendency to recur. Rare cases of metastasis, predominantly to the lungs, have also been reported. In the cervical spine, GCTB often invades the spinal canal and neural structures, causing pain, neurological dysfunction, or pathological fractures.

Rarely these lesions can rarely arise in the orbit.[39] Although benign, these lesions can potentially be locally aggressive and destructive.[40] Giant cell granulomas are more often diagnosed in women within the first two decades of life.[41] Recent studies have treated GCRG by sculpting the bone and removing the abnormal tissue without sharp excision.[40]
